title: Industry Collaboration and Student Development in Higher Education: Student Happiness Through Challenge
content: This study examines how industry collaboration and challenge-based learning, grounded in experiential learning principles, relate to student happiness, academic engagement-learning quality, and professional confidence. The empirical analysis draws on an anonymous survey of 210 students at the Faculty of Business Management of Vilniaus kolegija / Higher Education Institution, including 179 Lithuanian students and 31 international students. The instrument included 47 Likert-type items and one 10-point overall happiness item. Reliability analysis, descriptive statistics, Welch group comparisons, correlation analysis, OLS regression, and bootstrap mediation analysis were conducted. The results show that company visits (M = 4.05) and guest lectures or industry examples (M = 3.93) were evaluated most positively. However, these highly valued industry-oriented activities did not directly predict overall happiness in the regression analysis. The strongest unique predictors were academic engagement-learning quality, work-study balance, peer/social-psychological support, academic support, and academic community engagement. Mediation analysis indicated that industry engagement was associated with happiness indirectly through academic engagement-learning quality. An unexpected internationalization pattern was also observed: international students evaluated activities with an international dimension more positively than Lithuanian students but reported lower overall happiness. The study contributes to business management education research by showing that industry engagement alone is insufficient; student happiness emerges when real-world learning is transformed into meaningful and supported educational experiences.
